name: let's / shall I (polite)
english: Let's...; with ka, shall we...? or shall I...?
use: Polite suggestions, and offers of help: mochimashou ka? (shall I carry it?).
formation: Swap -masu for -mashou: tabemashou, ikimashou. suru → shimashou, kuru → kimashou. Add ka to offer or suggest more softly.

example.romaji: sono nimotsu, omoi deshou? mochimashou ka
example.ja: その荷物、重いでしょう？持ちましょうか。
example.english: That bag looks heavy. Shall I carry it?

notes: To invite someone, -masen ka is softer; -mashou assumes they'll say yes.

name: polite invitation
english: Won't you...? Would you like to...?
use: Inviting someone politely while leaving them room to say no.
formation: -masen plus ka: tabemasen ka, ikimasen ka. suru → shimasen ka, kuru → kimasen ka.

example.romaji: kondo, issho ni gohan tabemasen ka?
example.ja: 今度、一緒にご飯食べませんか？
example.english: Would you like to get a meal together sometime?

notes: Despite the negative, it's an invitation. The casual version is -nai? with a rising tone (ikanai?).

name: if / when
english: If..., or when (once)..., then something happens.
use: The everyday 'if' and 'when (once)': the conditional to reach for first.
formation: Make the -ta form and add ra: tabetara, kattara, nondara, ittara. suru → shitara, kuru → kitara.

example.ja: 駅に着いたら、連絡して。
example.english: Let me know when you get to the station.

examplePolite.romaji: eki ni tsuitara, renraku shite kudasai
examplePolite.ja: 駅に着いたら、連絡してください。
examplePolite.english: Please let me know when you get to the station.

notes: On its own with a rising tone it's advice: yasundara? = why don't you take a break?

name: if (condition)
use: Conditions and advice; -ba ii means 'you just have to' or 'you should'.
formation: Ichidan: drop ru, add reba (tabereba, mireba). Godan: change the last u to e, add ba (kaeba, nomeba, ikeba). suru → sureba, kuru → kureba.

example.english: You should just ask the teacher.

examplePolite.romaji: sensei ni kikeba ii desu yo
examplePolite.ja: 先生に聞けばいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: You can just ask the teacher.

notes: For a one-off 'when / after', -tara is more natural; keep -ba for conditions and -ba ii advice.

name: whenever / if (automatic)
english: Whenever or if X happens, Y follows naturally.
use: Directions, how things work, and habits: migi ni magaru to... (turn right and...).
formation: Dictionary form plus to: taberu to, kau to, iku to. suru → suru to, kuru → kuru to. For the negative, -nai to.

example.romaji: kono botan osu to, denki tsuku yo
example.ja: このボタン押すと、電気つくよ。
example.english: Press this button and the light comes on.

examplePolite.romaji: kono botan o osu to, denki ga tsukimasu
examplePolite.ja: このボタンを押すと、電気がつきます。
examplePolite.english: If you press this button, the light comes on.

notes: No requests or plans after it: say tsuitara renraku shite, not tsuku to renraku shite.

name: if that's the case
english: If that's the case; if you're going to...
use: Reacting to what someone just said, often with advice.
formation: Dictionary form plus nara: taberu nara, kau nara, iku nara. suru → suru nara, kuru → kuru nara. It also follows nouns and the -nai form.

example.romaji: kyouto iku nara, kasa motte itte
example.ja: 京都行くなら、傘持っていって。
example.english: If you're going to Kyoto, take an umbrella.

examplePolite.romaji: kyouto ni iku nara, kasa o motte itte kudasai
examplePolite.ja: 京都に行くなら、傘を持っていってください。
examplePolite.english: If you're going to Kyoto, please take an umbrella.

notes: nara looks ahead: iku nara = if you're going (advice before you go); ittara = once you've gone.

name: have to
use: Casual -nakya (or -nakucha) for what you've got to do. The full -nakereba naranai is formal.
formation: Make the -nai form, then swap nai for nakya (or nakereba): tabenakya, kawanakya, ikanakya. suru → shinakya, kuru → konakya. The 'or else' ending (ikenai, naranai) is usually dropped in speech.

example.ja: やばい、もう行かなきゃ。またね。
example.english: Yikes, I've got to go. See you.

examplePolite.ja: すみません、もう行かなければなりません。
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry, I have to go now.

notes: Don't mix it up with -nakute mo ii: ikanakya = I have to go; ikanakute mo ii = I don't have to go.

name: not, and / don't have to
english: Not ... and; because (it's) not ...; with mo ii, don't have to.
use: Giving a reason something didn't work out, and with mo ii, telling someone they don't need to.
formation: Make the -nai form, then swap nai for nakute: tabenakute, kawanakute, ikanakute. suru → shinakute, kuru → konakute.

example.romaji: kyou wa konakute mo ii yo
example.ja: 今日は来なくてもいいよ。
example.english: You don't have to come today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa konakute mo ii desu yo
examplePolite.ja: 今日は来なくてもいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: You don't need to come today.

notes: For 'please don't', use -naide, not -nakute: tabenaide (don't eat it).

name: may / it's OK to
use: Asking for permission (-te mo ii?) and giving it.
formation: te-form plus mo ii: tabete mo ii, katte mo ii, nonde mo ii. suru → shite mo ii, kuru → kite mo ii.

examplePolite.romaji: kore, tabete mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: これ、食べてもいいですか？

notes: In speech mo often drops: tabete ii? = can I eat it?

name: mustn't
use: Casual 'you can't do that', often to children or close friends.
formation: It's -te wa squeezed together: -te → -cha, -de → -ja, then add dame: tabecha dame, katcha dame, nonja dame. suru → shicha dame, kuru → kicha dame.

example.romaji: koko de shashin totcha dame da yo
example.ja: ここで写真撮っちゃだめだよ。

examplePolite.romaji: koko de shashin o totte wa ikemasen
examplePolite.ja: ここで写真を撮ってはいけません。

notes: Don't confuse it with -chau (did, often by accident): tabechatta = I ate it all; tabecha dame = don't eat it.
